# Preface {#sec-about .unnumbered}

## Who This Book Is For {#sec-book-audience .unlisted}

This book is for machine learning researchers, robotics engineers, embedded systems architects, and students who want to build embodied intelligent systems that safely sense, reason, and act in the physical universe.

When a model is evaluated on stored examples, its predictions do not change those examples. An autonomous vehicle can use a model's output to steer, changing where it moves and what its sensors observe next. The vehicle also keeps moving while the computer processes an observation. Assessing the model therefore requires understanding how sensing, computation, and movement work together.

This book provides the systems foundations for **Physical AI**: the engineering discipline of designing, running, and governing machine learning systems under the non-negotiable constraints of Newtonian mechanics, real-time deadlines, thermal limits, and physical safety. Its focus is the complete system, the interactions among its components, and the engineering decisions those interactions require. It introduces necessary concepts from robotics, control, and embedded systems through mechanisms and concrete tasks, without assuming specialist expertise in those disciplines. Detailed derivations and implementation material provide optional depth; the main explanation remains understandable without them.

---

## Why a Physical AI Systems Textbook {#sec-book-why-physical .unlisted}

A robot approaching an obstacle uses some of the available distance while its computer processes a sensor observation. At constant speed, the distance traveled during computation is the speed multiplied by computation time.

$$d_{\text{displacement}} = v \cdot t_{\text{compute}}$$

A mobile robot traveling at a constant 3 m/s travels 600 millimeters during 200 ms of model computation. This measures travel during computation; additional response delays and braking require further distance. Doubling the computation time at the same speed doubles that travel. A late result leaves less room to respond, so operating speed must be considered together with processing time, available space, and braking ability.

The response involves more than the learned model. The model can propose slowing down, but the body must generate the braking force, and the communication and control system must turn the proposal into a timely command. Stronger brakes cannot recover distance already traveled during computation, and a faster model cannot make the body stop instantaneously. The model's timing and the body's response must therefore be assessed together.

Before a proposed command reaches the body, a checking component can compare it with limits based on the available space and the machine's motion. A command to accelerate toward an obstacle can be rejected when it would leave too little distance to stop under the system's model of motion. The design must also specify how to respond to a rejected command. Any protection these checks provide depends on accurate observations, valid physical assumptions, and timely execution. These dependencies are why the book treats learned behavior, mechanical design, and execution as parts of one system.

## What This Book Covers {#sec-book-structure .unlisted}

The introduction frames the engineering problem for the whole book. Four parts then move from machine anatomy to field release:

*   **Part I: The Machine Anatomy** establishes how the physical body responds to commands, how the nervous system carries and executes them in time, and how the cognitive brain proposes actions.
*   **Part II: Teaching the Machine** covers physical data collection, learning behavior from that experience, and evaluating the resulting behavior as the machine's actions change what it observes next.
*   **Part III: Running the Machine** details runtime execution, from sensing and remembering the surroundings to selecting goals, planning and checking motion, and assigning computation to the hardware that must execute it.
*   **Part IV: Governing the Machine** addresses how to supervise a machine, test its behavior under difficult conditions, and assess the evidence needed to decide whether it is ready for release.

The conclusion brings these engineering decisions together and considers the limits of current understanding.

The physical AI stack maps these topics from learned proposals through real-time execution to the physical world. A recurring margin figure highlights the layers each chapter addresses, keeping its focus in view within the complete system.

## Related Books in the Machine Learning Systems Curriculum {#sec-book-series-map .unlisted}

This book is part of the *Machine Learning Systems* curriculum. *Introduction to Machine Learning Systems* examines how models use computation and memory on a single machine. *Scaling Machine Learning Systems* extends that engineering scope to coordinating work across many machines.

The curriculum also addresses systems that take actions. *Agentic Machine Learning Systems* focuses on action in digital environments, while *Physical AI Systems* examines actions that produce motion and change conditions in the physical world. The books offer complementary perspectives. This volume stands on its own, introducing the concepts needed to reason about the complete physical system.
